guide.summary: Calendly documents OAuth apps using authorization code flow with PKCE for per-user access across multiple accounts. The `event_types:read` scope covers GET /event_types for listing event types and does not include write or organization administration.

findings.title: OAuth with PKCE required for multi-account apps
findings.detail: OAuth is required for apps used by multiple accounts; personal access tokens are for a single account. Each user authorizes via the authorization code flow with S256 PKCE, and the server exchanges the code at /oauth/token with the client secret. Access tokens expire after 2 hours; refresh tokens are single-use and rotate.
findings.appliesWhen: Customer accounts each authorize the app individually.

steps.title: Register the OAuth app in Calendly Developer tools
steps.detail: Log in to Calendly, open Profile menu > Developer, then the OAuth apps tab > Create OAuth app. Enter an app name (letters, numbers, hyphens, spaces only), exactly one redirect URI and an environment type. Sandbox allows https and http on localhost; Production allows https only. Use a separate Sandbox app for development. Select only event_types:read, then Create. Anyone with a Calendly account can register.
steps.doneWhen: The OAuth app appears in the OAuth apps tab with the chosen environment, one redirect URI and the event_types:read scope.

evidence.quote: 3. On the **OAuth apps** tab, select **Create OAuth app**.
* **Redirect URI**: the URL where Calendly sends users after they authorize your app. Enter exactly one URI.
5. Select **Next**. 6. Select the scopes that your app needs. Select at least one scope. Learn more about scopes.

steps.title: Save client ID, client secret and webhook signing key
steps.detail: Calendly shows the client ID, client secret and webhook signing key once after creation. Copy all three into a secrets manager before leaving the screen. They cannot be viewed again. The client secret is used only by your server.
steps.doneWhen: Client ID and client secret are stored in server-side secret storage and not in client code or logs.

* **Client ID**: your app's identifier. Send it in each OAuth request.
* **Client secret**: a secret that your server uses to authenticate with Calendly.

steps.title: Implement the server callback and PKCE generation
steps.detail: Implement an HTTPS callback at the exact registered redirect URI (http://localhost only in Sandbox). Per authorization attempt, generate a CODE_VERIFIER and an S256 CODE_CHALLENGE (SHA-256), and store the verifier server-side keyed to the signed-in app user. The agent can draft this code; the developer implements and deploys it. PKCE is mandatory or the request fails.
steps.doneWhen: The callback route is reachable at the registered redirect URI and PKCE verifier/challenge generation is unit-tested.

evidence.quote: Every OAuth app must use Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) with the `S256` method. If the authorization request does not include a code challenge, the request fails. For more
1. Generate a `CODE_VERIFIER`.
2. Build a `CODE_CHALLENGE` from the verifier with SHA-256.

steps.title: Send the connected user to the consent page
steps.detail: Redirect the user's browser to the authorization URL; it must be requested in a web browser. Required parameters: client_id, response_type=code, redirect_uri, code_challenge_method=S256, code_challenge. Request only the scope event_types:read (space-separated scopes parameter). The user can decline scopes. The docs do not state state-parameter handling or an account-choice screen. Bind the returned code to your signed-in app user via a stored session/verifier so one person's grant cannot overwrite another's.
steps.doneWhen: The browser lands on the redirect URI with ?code=... after the representative user approves.

evidence.quote: ``` https://auth.calendly.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=CLIENT_ID&response_type=code&redirect_uri=com.site.app://auth/calendly&code_challenge_method=S256&code_challenge=CODE_CHALLENGE ``` After the user grants access, they will be redirected back to
&response_type=code &scope=scheduled_events:read webhooks:write ```
Parameter code_challenge in query (string, required): The PKCE code challenge, built from your code verifier with SHA-256. Required for every app. Schema: {"type":"string"}

steps.title: Validate the callback before exchanging the code
steps.detail: On the callback, confirm the request matches an in-progress authorization for the signed-in app user, extract the code query parameter, and load the stored code_verifier for that attempt. Reject callbacks with no matching pending attempt. Do not log the code.
steps.doneWhen: The callback handler extracts code and finds the matching stored verifier for the user's session.

evidence.quote: &code_challenge_method=S256 &code_challenge=CODE_CHALLENGE ``` After the user grants access, Calendly redirects the user to your redirect URI with the authorization code:
```http REDIRECT_URI?code=f04281d639d8248435378b0365de7bd1f53bf452eda187d5f1e07ae7f04546d6 ``` ### Exchange the code for an access token

steps.title: Exchange the code for tokens on the server
steps.detail: Run on your server only. POST to the token endpoint with HTTP Basic auth (client ID as username, client secret as password) and body fields grant_type=authorization_code, code, redirect_uri (same as used for the code), client_id and code_verifier. Store access_token and refresh_token encrypted, keyed to the authorizing user (response owner) and organization. Access tokens last 2 hours; refresh tokens are single-use, so overwrite the stored one on every refresh.
steps.doneWhen: The response contains access_token, refresh_token, owner and organization, and they are stored encrypted under that user.

If your app runs on a server, also send your client secret. Use HTTP Basic authentication with your client ID as the username and your client secret as the password.
Note: * Access Tokens expire after 2 hours.

steps.title: Test with a representative account
steps.detail: Authorize with a Sandbox app and a representative Calendly account, then confirm only event_types:read is granted. Run two refresh cycles: use refresh token R1, store R2, confirm R1 is rejected, and use R2 again. Confirm a second test user's grant is stored separately.
steps.doneWhen: Authorization succeeds, event type names are shown, the old refresh token is rejected and two users hold separate stored grants.

evidence.quote: Go through a token refresh cycle twice in a row. Use refresh token R1 to get a new token (response gives you R2). Any attempt to reuse R1 should be
* **Immediately overwrites** the stored refresh token with the new `refresh_token` from every successful `POST /oauth/token` response.
If your code reuses an old refresh token, the Calendly API will respond with HTTP 400 or 401 and the JSON error `invalid_grant`. This means the token was already used
